scenes.tts: Can you watch the cerebellum learn? Put on prism goggles, and throw.
scenes.visual: Title card fades. A person in prism goggles faces a target board. The question appears.
scenes.narration: Can you watch the cerebellum learn? Put on prism goggles, and throw.

scenes.tts: The goggles shift what you see to the right. So the first throws miss to the right.
scenes.visual: The view through the goggles slides right. The first dot lands well right of the bullseye.
scenes.narration: The goggles shift what you see to the right. So the first throws miss to the right.

scenes.tts: Each miss teaches a little. Throw by throw, the misses walk in toward the target.
scenes.visual: Dots march from right toward the centre. Beside the board, an error versus throw curve draws, falling steeply then levelling. The axes carry the numbers; none are spoken. Small label: toy model, not patient data.
scenes.narration: Each miss teaches a little. Throw by throw, the misses walk in toward the target.

scenes.tts: How much each error teaches sets how fast this curve falls. Call it k, the fraction of the error corrected per throw.
scenes.visual: The curve's step from one throw to the next is highlighted and labelled: k = fraction of remaining error corrected per throw.
scenes.narration: How much each error teaches sets how fast this curve falls. Call it k, the fraction of the error corrected per throw.

scenes.tts: Now take the goggles off. Where does the next throw land?
scenes.visual: The goggles lift away. The board waits for the next throw. Question on screen: Goggles off. Where does it land?
scenes.narration: Now take the goggles off. Where does the next throw land?

scenes.tts: To the left. The learned correction is still being applied, to a world that has changed back. That opposite miss is the after effect.
scenes.caption: To the left. The learned correction is still being applied, to a world that has changed back. That opposite miss is the after-effect.
scenes.visual: One dot lands left of the bullseye. Label: after-effect = the learned correction, still being applied.
scenes.narration: To the left. The learned correction is still being applied, to a world that has changed back. That opposite miss is the after-effect.

scenes.tts: It shows that the mapping between seeing and moving was recalibrated.
scenes.visual: A link between an eye and a hand is redrawn. Small note: includes shifts in where you see and feel your arm.
scenes.narration: It shows that the mapping between seeing and moving was recalibrated.

scenes.tts: Real after effects are usually smaller, partly because people drop a deliberate aiming strategy once the goggles are off.
scenes.caption: Real after-effects are usually smaller, partly because people drop a deliberate aiming strategy once the goggles are off.
scenes.visual: The left dot slides a little back toward centre. Label: smaller in real throwers, partly from dropping a deliberate aiming strategy.
scenes.narration: Real after-effects are usually smaller, partly because people drop a deliberate aiming strategy once the goggles are off.

scenes.tts: In people with damage to the olivo cerebellar system, adaptation at this task was impaired.
scenes.caption: In people with damage to the olivocerebellar system, adaptation at this task was impaired.
scenes.visual: Caption card: Martin and colleagues, 1996. Olivocerebellar damage: prism adaptation impaired.
scenes.narration: In people with damage to the olivocerebellar system, adaptation at this task was impaired.

scenes.tts: In the model, a smaller k means smaller steps. The curve flattens, and after the same number of throws the after effect is smaller too. The model does not say which part is damaged.
scenes.caption: In the model, a smaller k means smaller steps. The curve flattens, and after the same number of throws the after-effect is smaller too. The model does not say which part is damaged.
scenes.visual: A second, shallower curve draws beside the first, labelled small k, toy model of slow adaptation. With goggles off after the same number of throws, the patient's dot lands only a little left. Label: smaller after-effect at the same throw count.
scenes.narration: In the model, a smaller k means smaller steps. The curve flattens, and after the same number of throws the after-effect is smaller too. The model does not say which part is damaged.

scenes.tts: One account: lose the cerebellum's prediction, and the arm leans on slow feedback. Movements can overshoot and swing near the target.
scenes.visual: The overshooting, oscillating reach from the first chapter returns, its path traced beside it. Label: one proposed contributor.
scenes.narration: One account: lose the cerebellum's prediction, and the arm leans on slow feedback. Movements can overshoot and swing near the target.

scenes.tts: Now the side. A patient has a lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Which arm is more likely to show tremor?
scenes.visual: A front-view body map with the brain above. The left cerebellar hemisphere is shaded as damaged. Question on screen: Which arm?
scenes.narration: Now the side. A patient has a lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Which arm is more likely to show tremor?

scenes.tts: The left arm. Cerebellar output crosses to the right thalamus, which relays to the right motor cortex.
scenes.visual: An arrow leaves the left cerebellum and crosses the midline in the midbrain to the right thalamus, then on to right motor cortex. Label: crossing 1.
scenes.narration: The left arm. Cerebellar output crosses to the right thalamus, which relays to the right motor cortex.

scenes.tts: Then the corticospinal tract crosses back, to the left side of the spinal cord. Two crossings cancel.
scenes.visual: A second arrow runs down from right cortex and crosses back in the caudal medulla to the left side of the cord. Label: crossing 2. The left arm highlights.
scenes.narration: Then the corticospinal tract crosses back, to the left side of the spinal cord. Two crossings cancel.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the cerebellum helps learn predictions from error. Damage can leave a limb leaning more on late feedback, one cause of clumsiness, on the same side.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: Helps learn predictions from error. Damage: more reliance on late feedback, one contributor to limb clumsiness, on the same side (pathways cross twice).
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the cerebellum helps learn predictions from error. Damage can leave a limb leaning more on late feedback, one cause of clumsiness, on the same side.
